💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that hospital ratings have become an important resource for choosing where to receive care.
  • On October 27, Healthgrades confirmed the recipients of the 2027 Specialty Excellence Outpatient Awards and Specialty State Rankings.
  • The annual awards recognize hospitals delivering outstanding patient outcomes in specialty care across the United States.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that hospital ratings have become an important resource for choosing where to receive care. They influence which doctors patients choose, how far they are willing to travel, and whether they seek care at a different facility.

On October 27, Healthgrades confirmed the recipients of the 2027 Specialty Excellence Outpatient Awards and Specialty State Rankings.

The annual awards recognize hospitals delivering outstanding patient outcomes in specialty care across the United States. Healthgrades is the leading platform used by Americans for finding a doctor or hospital.

Newly introduced research from Healthgrades highlights that hospital quality is increasingly a factor in healthcare decisions.

According to recent reports, around 80% of patients report that when looking for a doctor, the quality of the hospital where they practice matters. Additionally, 7 in 10 patients (68%) say they’re more likely to seek care for a procedure or health condition from a doctor who works at a hospital with high quality ratings.

What’s more, around 71% of patients say they would switch doctors to gain access to a higher-rated hospital.

“Our specialty awards identify the nation’s top-performing hospitals across numerous medical specialties, helping consumers find high quality care tailored to their specific needs,” mentioned Alana Biggers, MD, MPH, medical advisor at Healthgrades.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

“Navigating the complex healthcare system can feel daunting, but taking a proactive stance to understand where to access superior care can enhance your healthcare journey and overall experience. The ability to make informed decisions about your health — and where to get care — is a cornerstone of self-advocacy, and we are proud to help make that information accessible to all patients.”.

Healthgrades identifies hospitals that deliver exceptional outcomes across common outpatient procedures and specialty conditions.

Finding high quality care is crucial, particularly amid a growing gap between top-performing and one-star hospitals.

According to Healthgrades, from 2023 to 2025, if all hospitals had performed at the five-star level from 2023 to 2025:.

“One of the biggest challenges is balancing increasing patient needs with the resources available to healthcare professionals,” Biggers stated.

“Hospitals face workforce shortages, growing administrative responsibilities, financial pressures, and increasing complexity in patient care. Physicians and other healthcare professionals need adequate time and support not only to evaluate and treat patients, but also to communicate results, coordinate follow-up care, and address concerns that arise between visits,” she continued.

“When healthcare teams are adequately supported, they are better positioned to communicate effectively with patients, coordinate care, and address patients’ needs.”.

Biggers said that ensuring equal access to quality healthcare is challenging because of factors such as:.

Hospital closures and reduced services make access even more difficult. Biggers identified a few possible solutions, such as expanding outpatient care, building community partnerships, using telehealth when appropriate, and improving coordination among healthcare providers.

Recent findings suggest that “Ultimately, providing high quality care requires more than clinical expertise. It requires healthcare systems to invest in their workforce, strengthen care coordination, and create environments where healthcare professionals have the resources they need to provide safe, effective, and patient-centered care,” Biggers remarked.

“Equally important, healthcare systems must ensure that patients have meaningful access to these services, regardless of where they live or their socioeconomic circumstances.”.

Healthgrades acknowledges hospitals that excel in three aspects of specialty care:.

Biggers stated that outstanding hospitals recognize that high quality care extends beyond just treating an illness.

“It involves listening to patients, understanding their individual circumstances, and ensuring they feel respected, informed, and involved in their healthcare decisions,” she said.

Patients want to find a hospital that excels in the procedures or health conditions relevant to them.

The recipients of the Specialty Excellence Awards are among the top 15% of hospitals specializing in these areas.

Healthgrades evaluated patient outcomes at roughly 4,500 hospitals across 31 common procedures and conditions to reach their decisions.

Among the list of Specialty Excellence Award recipients, Healthgrades also recognizes America’s 100 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for 11 specialty areas andAmerica’s 50 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for four specialty areas.

“An outstanding hospital prioritizes both patient care and the people delivering that care,” Biggers told Healthline.

Industry observers note that “While clinical outcomes, patient safety, and access to evidence-based treatments are essential measures of quality, I believe hospitals must also invest in workforce development and support. This means ensuring physicians, nurses, and other healthcare professionals have appropriate staffing levels, adequate clinical and administrative support, and opportunities for continued professional development,” she continued.

Healthgrades awards U.S. hospitals that excel at Outpatient Orthopedic Surgery, Outpatient Joint Replacement, andOutpatient Prostate Care.

Outpatient care is one of the fastest-growing areas of healthcare. The number of orthopedic procedures performed in an outpatient environment has grown exponentially in recent years.

In a recent development, from 2020 to 2025, outpatient hip replacement procedures grew by 81%, while inpatient procedures dropped by 75%. Outpatient knee replacements increased by 71% while inpatient volumes decreased by 70%.

“I believe several factors are contributing to the growing demand for outpatient care, including advances in medical technology, a greater emphasis on preventive care, and the increasing need to manage chronic medical conditions,” Biggers said.

According to recent reports, “Many services and procedures that previously required hospitalization can now be safely performed in outpatient settings. Patients also appreciate the convenience of receiving care closer to home and avoiding unnecessary hospital stays,” she added.

To meet the increasing demand for outpatient procedures, Biggers cautioned that healthcare systems must ensure that these services are adequately staffed and supported.

“Effective communication and coordination between outpatient providers, specialists, and hospitals are essential to maintaining continuity and quality of care,” she stated.

State Rankings identify the top three or five hospitals in eligible states across 19 key specialty areas.

According to recent reports, healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

The rankings are based on clinical performance and build on the 2027 Healthgrades Specialty Excellence Awards Methodology.

State-level specialty care rankings help consumers find outstanding local hospitals for their condition or procedure.

The analysis used Medicare inpatient data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) from 2023 to 2025, and assessed patient outcomes across 31 conditions and procedures.

These outcomes served as the foundation for determining Specialty Excellence Awards and state hospital rankings.

With consumer-facing awards and ratings influencing healthcare decisions, transparency about their methods and limitations remains essential.

Ratings can help patients ask better questions and compare options, but they should complement — not replace — clinical guidance and informed decision making.

The methodologies for each of the specialty awards can be found on the following pages:.

In a recent development, for more information, Healthgrades’ Specialty Excellence Patient Advocate Center provides access to the information you need to make informed decisions about your care. This resource includes an overview of how Healthgrades picks award recipients, plus a list of the top U.S. hospitals for specialty care.

To be eligible for a Specialty Excellence Award, hospitals must receive a rating in the required procedures and conditions used to determine the award. Some awards are based on a single procedure, while others are based on a grouping of procedures. To learn more about Healthgrades’ ratings and awards determination process, see the 2027 Specialty Excellence Awards and Ratings Methodology.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dongfeng Nissan officially opened the early order book on its fresh NX7 hybrid yesterday, promising up to 320 km (~198 miles) of all-electric range from a 40 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery and a $20,000 price tag.

Industry observers note that when the first generation Nissan LEAF bowed with 70-ish miles of range from its 24 kWh li-ion battery pack, it struggled to meet widespread adoption, especially in an SUV-obsessed US market that demands forethought-free trips to Home Depot and bladder-busting range. The organization’s latest 2027 Rogue Hybrid is a step in the right direction, using a gas engine to generate electricity for a pair of electric drive motors that deliver a driving experience that’s remarkably similar to a “pure” electric car – but without a plug, it’s still entirely dependent on fossil fuels. The new Dongfeng Nissan NX7, though? That’s a different story.

According to recent reports, the plug-in hybrid Dongfeng Nissan NX7 might be called a “long range hybrid” in the same sense that Volvo’s Euro-market XC70 is, in that it’s an EV for the 360-odd days a year that you’re driving less than 200 miles, and an ICE vehicle for the handful of days you drive more. And if you’re one of those people who thinks stopping on road trips is a character flaw, a fully charged and topped off NX7 will take you an astonishing 1,666 km (~1,035 miles) from where you started.

The new NX7 could be an ideal lilypad vehicle for North American drivers who are either too afraid of being caught without a charger or too invested in the outcome of one or more dumb oil wars to confidently make the switch to EV – and, even at twice the 129,900 yuan ($~19,400) asking price, I think it would be a hit.

For that money, NX7 buyers get an absolutely loaded Model Y-sized crossover (they’re within 1/4″ of each other in length), with a 17.3″ central touchscreen, a fully digital instrument cluster, and (on higher-spec models) a positively massive 55″ augmented-reality head-up display powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8295P automotive processor and running on Nissan OS 3.0 with an AI-powered voice assistant developed with iFlytek that, Nissan claims, can recognize natural-language commands, remember user preferences, and even recognize occupants, adjusting vehicle settings accordingly.

Sources indicate that on top-shelf models, the NX7 cabins get “AI Zero-Pressure Cloud Blanket” seats that use sensors and air-cushion arrays to dynamically adjust for maximum comfort, and include heating, ventilation, and a 12-point SPA-level massage function. The front seats can be fully reclined to create a bed-like configuration that will be familiar to Cube owners. The NX7 even offers an on-board refrigerator and motion-sickness prevention system that Nissan claims can reduce motion sickness by as much as 83% (which, like, I wouldn’t want to be the one to test that – but seems cool).

Recent findings suggest that power comes from a 1.5-liter naturally aspirated internal combustion engine making 98 hp that’s paired to a 228 hp electric drive motor and the previously mentioned 40.9 kWh LFP battery. It’s not immediately clear if the NX7 uses a conventional parallel hybrid system like a Prius or a series-hybrid-plus-plug setup, but Dongfeng’s hybrid technology patents describe a pretty versatile arrangement with four possible operating modes: series hybrid, parallel hybrid, direct engine drive and electricity generation – which means the vehicle can theoretically use the ICE motor as a generator, drive the wheels mechanically, or work alongside the electric motor, depending on what the operating conditions call for. Whether any or all four modes make it to production on the NX7 remains to be seen, but it’s an intriguing bit of engineering for a vehicle promising nearly 200 miles of electric driving range.

Why is this article written like it will be available in the US market? It’s made in China and has Chinese software, we’ll never see it.

The final production version will be shown to the public for the first time at the Guangzhou Auto Show later this month, but you can let us know what you think of the newly introduced NX7 in the comments, today.

#29702. Robo-frog swims with liquid crystal muscles powered by light

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (453 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Robo-frog swims with liquid crystal muscles powered by light

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (453 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A silicone frog built by engineers at Denmark’s Aarhus University can’t swim nearly as fast as its amphibian inspiration, but it still manages to get the job done without any moving parts.
  • The team’s novel system is detailed in a study recently published in the journal Advanced Materials Technologies.
  • “I could easily imagine these robots being used as toys before we see them on rescue missions,” Cecilie Ryberg, Aarhus University chemist and study co-author, mentioned in a profile.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A silicone frog built by engineers at Denmark’s Aarhus University can’t swim nearly as fast as its amphibian inspiration, but it still manages to get the job done without any moving parts. The odd invention owes its slow-but-steady aquatic maneuvering to a set of six artificial muscles specially designed to contract when exposed to near-infrared light.

The team’s novel system is detailed in a study recently published in the journal Advanced Materials Technologies. Although similar setups may one day boost the capabilities of soft robots tasked with search and rescue or environmental monitoring, its creators are a bit more realistic about this frog-bot’s near-term uses.

“I could easily imagine these robots being used as toys before we see them on rescue missions,” Cecilie Ryberg, Aarhus University chemist and study co-author, mentioned in a profile. “I think people would have fun playing with a frog like this using a suitable light source.”.

Each of the robot’s muscles is built using crystal elastomers. These materials are specifically manufactured to contract while they are heating, and then revert back to their original shape once cooled. In this case, Ryberg and her collaborators also added a molecule that converts near-infrared light into heat. This allows the muscles to tighten after directly exposing them to a lamp. That mentioned, the process isn’t as simple as sticking the elastomers onto their model frog and dropping it into water.

Sources indicate that “Getting the six muscles to work together was a major challenge,” explained Brigitte Städler, a study co-author and Aarhus University chemist. “If they don’t contract in a coordinated way, the frog won’t swim forwards. It may simply spin around.”.

A lot of trial-and-error also went into concocting the elastomers themselves. In addition to contracting properly, the material needed the proper consistency to use in a 3D printer. To do this, Ryberg experimented with various molecular ingredients and molecule chain lengths to perfect the robot muscle recipe.

Recent findings suggest that “In a conventional 3D printer, you typically melt a solid plastic filament. Our material is more like very thick syrup or icing that you squeeze through a piping bag when decorating a cake,” said Ryberg.

The final result is a light-powered soft robot that’s quite unique, but also not in any hurry. At its best pace, the frog swam a little over three inches in about two minutes. That may not get it to its destination quickly, but the proof-of-concept successfully offers a upcoming way to think about robotic design, and the ways engineers can power their creations. Until then, there is always the potential for robo-frog toys.

#29701. The Electric BMW M3 Delivers Thrills, Synthesized Sounds, and Pretend Gears

The Electric BMW M3 Delivers Thrills, Synthesized Sounds, and Pretend Gears

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2098 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that attend an event organized by BMW’s M Division, and you know what you are going to get.
  • In a recent development, but then, as the noise grew louder, the narrative shifted.
  • Sources indicate that we’ve known for some time that the BMW M3 was going to make the switch to becoming an EV, but the reality of what that entails for those watching from outside the car was still a mild shock.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that attend an event organized by BMW’s M Division, and you know what you are going to get. Such as plentiful M branding everywhere. It was no surprise when I arrived at BMW’s proving ground in Miramar, France, to experience the M3 prototype for the first time to see numerous flags and banners with the famous slant “M” logo. And it felt equally natural for a moment to be listening to the sound of a hard-worked engine on the test track, with what seemed the entirely M-appropriate howl of a straight-six exhaling through a minimally muffled exhaust.

In a recent development, but then, as the noise grew louder, the narrative shifted. Because it was an M4 GT4 making the compelling racket. The two M3 prototypes that followed it wearing a vibrant, dazzle pattern disguise, were traveling every bit as swiftly but almost entirely silently.

Sources indicate that we’ve known for some time that the BMW M3 was going to make the switch to becoming an EV, but the reality of what that entails for those watching from outside the car was still a mild shock. The good news for anyone unsure about such a radical departure for the subbrand is that work on a gasoline-powered M3 is continuing in parallel. The combustion version, with the development code G85, is likely to feature another version of the S58 turbocharged inline-six from the current G80 generation, likely working in conjunction with some level of hybrid assistance. That will be a much more traditional take on the junior M car, but it almost certainly won’t be as powerful or as quick as the fully electric version.

But is our world ready for this level of different?

My first experience at Miramar was a passenger ride around the handling track, sitting in the left seat of one of the four colorfully-wrapped prototypes beside Sven Esch, M’s head of vehicle dynamics. I knew the car had a quad-motor powertrain, with one motor driving each wheel, and I could see it was riding on new Michelin Pilot Sport S 6 tires, but that was about all I had to go on when Esch executed a full launch-control start, one brutal enough to leave me confident the finished car will be another member of the two-second club when it comes to 0–60 times. The other disclosure, delivered from the changing tone of the noise coming from the speakers and the sight of Esch’s fingers working paddles behind the steering wheel, is that BMW is joining Hyundai, Porsche, and Mercedes in having a simulated gear system. The lap also revealed a handling balance familiar from many generations of M cars, with varying angles of oversteer through most of the corners.

It has been revealed that there are still many unknowns. Although the cars at Miramar were close to production spec, BMW is keeping many details to itself. There are no performance claims yet. And every number given for power, torque, range and charging speed carried an asterisk leading to an “approximately” proviso. The maximum system output was quoted at 838 hp and 885 lb-ft, with the pair of front motors able to deliver up to 643 hp and 398 lb-ft working together, while the larger two in back max out at a claimed 750 hp and 738 lb-ft. Given the way automotive PR typically works, I would be surprised if any of those figures grew any worse before becoming finalized. But they are clearly a way off the 1153-hp AMG GT 63 4-Door, the 1123-hp Lucid Air Sapphire, and the 1019-hp Porsche Taycan Turbo GT.

The M3 EV uses a different battery pack from the regular i3, with a newly introduced cell design and double-sided cooling to enable huge peak flow rates, with this having approximately 100 kWh of usable energy and operating at up to 800 volts. BMW is predicting an EPA range of 300 miles, and peak DC charging speeds will be around 420 kilowatts—slightly higher than the regular i3 and better than the speediest Taycan, but a way off the 600-kW capability of the AMG. More impressive is the ability of the battery pack to reabsorb energy through regeneration, doing this at rates of up to—approximately again—540 kilowatts. So the equivalent of 724 hp, without having to use the carbon-ceramic discs and pads.

It has been revealed that then there are the simulated gears. Although, pedantically, these are not. BMW has decided the mDrive mode allows the selection of what it calls “stages,” of which there are six. The default mode on startup is actually Automatic, in which the car changes between the stages by itself while playing a corresponding soundtrack as it does so, like a true automatic transmission in drive. There is also a paddle mode that gives you the ability to select a stage and also a simulated limiter if you fail to change up in time. It also has a normal EV single-speed drive mode.

It has been revealed that beneath the surface, the M3 has been given a substantial structural work over compared with the i3, the M version getting additional reinforcement for suspension subframes and also plates that bolt to the underfloor battery pack front and rear to better integrate this into the car’s structure. There is also a strut brace between the front suspension towers, eliminating the i3’s frunk, plus smaller reinforcement struts within the A-pillars and on the rear towers.

Industry observers note that while the M3 might be beaten by rivals on power statistics, it turns tables with the complexity of its powertrain. Having individual motors for each wheel is a segment first, in contrast with the two-motor Taycan Turbo GT and the three-motor AMG GT 4-Door and Lucid Air Sapphire. The lack of any physical connection between the different wheels means all the functions normally handled by differentials and clutch packs have to be done electronically, a hugely complex task for the dynamic control system. But it also brings benefits, most obvious is the ability to vary the torque going to each individual wheel almost instantly, without the response delay of even the fastest-acting mechanical systems. And it can also do this with regeneration, changing the braking effect on each wheel with equal dexterity.

In a recent development, my chance to experience all this witchcraft was limited to two stints on the Miramar handling track, following the raucous M4 GTS being piloted by works driver Jens Klingmann at a pretty gentle pace, and with Carsten Wolf, vehicle characteristics manager, riding shotgun. Wolf proved to be a pretty laid-back passenger, but I was only able to switch certain dynamic settings.

While the electric M3’s cabin architecture is very similar to that of the i3 and the newly introduced 3-series, the prototype wore a dashboard cover to obscure what I’m told were unfinished screen-layout designs. The car did have an M-specific version of BMW’s Panoramic Vision extra-long gauge cluster, which features a rendered “rev counter” very similar in design to the one in the new M350 xDrive, two graphic bars moving apart. There was also a small set of color-changing shift lights.

It has been revealed that it was immediately clear that performance was on another level to the i3 50 I had driven earlier the same day. The M3 felt every bit as quick as the power figures suggested it should, with none of the shortish straights of the handling track being long enough to bring any sense of acceleration beginning to tail off, even as speeds headed well north of 100 mph, and the M4 GT4 was visibly having to work hard to keep a gap. In a straightline fight, I’m certain the EV would have been the faster car, although riding on Pirelli slicks, and having Klingmann at the wheel, gave the car a clear advantage in corners.

Industry observers note that the M3’s steering was heavier than the i3 and M350’s and brought a far better sense of connection to the front tires. Unlike some cars with lots of electrical power going through the front axle, the prototype didn’t suffer from any steering corruption, albeit over what was generally a smooth track surface. Even in the softest Comfort mode, the car turned into corners with a keenness that was clearly being helped by applying different levels of regen to each wheel, which then kept it locked to a chosen line.

Or at least, it stayed locked until I started to try and get early onto the accelerator. At which point a newly introduced sensation arrived, unexpected in an M3: mild understeer. The control systems were clearly intervening hard in the background; winding off lock brought full fury back immediately. At Wolf’s suggestion, I pressed the steering wheel’s M1 button to shift the drivetrain and chassis to their Sport setting, reducing the front-end push.

But it required the M2 button, which brought the most aggressive Sport Plus settings, and putting the stability control into its half-off MDM mode to unlock the M3’s party spirit and show the side of its personality I’d first experienced from the passenger’s seat, with progressive, easily controllable oversteer.

Industry observers note that plenty of magic was still going on behind the scenes. I noticed that even if I wasn’t quick to apply opposite lock, the prototype would still hold a tidy drift, the dynamic brain carefully metering the torque going to each corner—I was in no doubt that turning the stability management fully off would be a different level of challenge. But, at last, the M3 was feeling like an M3 should.

It has been revealed that the wheel-by-wheel regeneration was much more subtle. The i3 already blends electrical and friction braking seamlessly, and the M3 is on a different level, able to use regen to the point of ABS intervention. The left pedal was firm and proportionate, and I had no sense of when one side was handing over to the other. But even under track loadings, most slowing was being done electrically. At the end of my first stint, Wolf, smiling, handed me an infrared temperature reader and invited me to measure the brake temperatures. At the front, the carbon disc was at just 100 degrees Celsius (212 degrees Fahrenheit), way less than I would expect after 10 minutes of track driving in an 800-hp car that weighs around 5000 pounds. The other advantage of the ability to harvest so much energy is a significant improvement to track range; Wolf indicates that for every three laps the car was recuperating enough for another lap at the same pace.

According to recent reports, what about the virtual gears? Sorry, the “stages.” These were less convincing. The sounds being piped over the M3’s speakers are loud and engine-like, especially at lower simulated revs, but they grow more otherworldly and sci-fi as the shift lights start to illuminate: I was detecting distinct notes of TIE fighter. M has deliberately taken a different direction from AMG, which has the GT 4-dr doing a full-fledged V-8 impression. BMW’s approach is arguably the more honest one; the M3 isn’t pretending to be something it isn’t.

But I noticed that the stages also had much less torque modeling than rivals such as Porsche’s E-Shift system in the Taycan, or the pioneering e-Shift in the Hyundai Ioniq 5N, which started this whole game. Beyond the possibility of hitting the M3’s artificial limiter, being in the wrong gear didn’t bring much obvious penalty on track. After a couple of laps of changing with the paddles, I actually went back to Automatic mode, where the virtual gears shift themselves. Which proved that the rising and falling soundtrack does help orientate corner entry speeds. Driving the slow-down lap with both the stepped gears and the speed sound turned off made the M3 prototype suddenly feel like a sensory deprivation chamber.

According to recent reports, what was a very limited first drive was clearly aimed at raising anticipation for the finished car more than answering every dynamic question. It was enough to prove that this M3 is a radical shift from its predecessors. But also to validate BMW’s claim that it is set to be the fastest and most powerful M car yet. The prototype also felt at home on a racetrack in a way that EVs very rarely do, and it has clearly been designed with circuit work in mind. This is a very, very different M3—and I’m glad there will still be a more traditional one. But the electric version still feels worthy of its famous badge.

#29700. Tech Report: Why the Word “Boundaries” Makes Boomer Parents Mad

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1233 w)

Tech Report: Why the Word “Boundaries” Makes Boomer Parents Mad

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1233 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.
  • According to recent reports, when the topic of boundaries comes up, a Millennial woman (born 1981-1996 according to Pew Research) will vigorously nod in agreement.
  • It has been revealed that how did a word meant to build healthier relationships become one that is so triggering?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

According to recent reports, when the topic of boundaries comes up, a Millennial woman (born 1981-1996 according to Pew Research) will vigorously nod in agreement. But when that same daughter tries to install those boundaries with her Baby Boomer mother, (born between 1946-1964, according to Pew Research), the reaction can be swift and negative: Mom gives a raised eyebrow, a long silence, or an extreme and snarky reply.

It has been revealed that how did a word meant to build healthier relationships become one that is so triggering? Why do boundaries make your family members feel rejected? The matter isn't the latest behavior and delineation itself, but what the word signals.

For some adult daughters (Gen X were born 1965-1980; Millennials born 1981-1996; and even adult Gen Z (born 1997-2012, according to Pew Research), boundaries represent a way to honor yourself, not give up on the elements in a relationship that matter to you, and hopefully reflect your evolving emotional maturity. For a Baby Boomer parent, boundary talk sounds like withdrawal, rejection, and pulling away from the family (or particularly from them).

Part of the problem is that the paradigm of “Boomers vs. Millennials” has become a ready-made cultural storyline. In a 2026 study of Instagram memes about the two generations, media researchers Centorrino and Ferrigno found that the largest group of memes did one thing above all: draw lines between generations. That is, sow division between the Millennial and the Boomer. These memes ranged from dismissive jokes like “OK Boomer” to side-by-side comparisons of what each generation was like at the same age, but with a negative twist. The researchers argue that generational labels work less like neutral categories and more like symbolic boundaries, sorting people into “us” and “them.” It can become a crass classification system or a way of saying "they're not like me and my peers.".

Industry observers note that with this culturally sensitive division in mind, when a daughter deploys the language of boundaries, her mother may not hear a healthy limit. She may hear one more line being drawn between “your generation” and “mine.” In short, she feels pushed away and made fun of for her behaviors and ways of doing things. That's a pretty substantial barrier to hearing their adult child in a neutral or healthy way.

Research on adult development helps explain why this mismatch runs so deep. Karen Fingerman, a leading researcher on parents and adult children, and her colleagues draw on socioemotional selectivity theory. This theory suggests that as people age, they become more invested in keeping their longest-standing close ties than in forming new ones. That means they get really zoned-in on their adult children, their own siblings, and lifelong close friends.

In a 2024 study of more than 300 adults aged 65 and older, Fingerman’s team found that nearly three-quarters of participants’ long-term relationships were with family. That means most of what an older person wants is from their adult kids. They're invested in these long-term relationships with a deep intensity. However, the parent-child ties were also complicated. The time older folks spent with their family members was linked to more stressful conversations and intense moods (both positive and negative). All this means that Boomer parents are putting an intense lens on their adult child and it's kind of stressful.

It has been revealed that and here's the rub. That intensity only goes one way. Researchers have described the concept of “intergenerational stake”: parents tend to be more invested in their children than children are in their parents. In a 2015 study of more than 600 middle-aged adults, Kira Birditt, Fingerman, and colleagues found that people rated their relationships with their children as both more important and more negative than their relationships with their own parents. Friction, in other words, can be a sign of how much a relationship matters. In sum, the more an adult child matters to their parent, the more likely there's tension as they seek connection.

Sources indicate that why does that friction occur? Fingerman’s earlier work points to an answer. In a 1996 study of 48 mothers over 70 and their middle-aged daughters, she introduced the term “developmental schism” to describe tension that arises because mothers and daughters are at different points in adult development. That's the sandpaper feeling between mothers and adult daughters, even when there's a lot of love. Two of the biggest sources of that tension were independence and how much importance each person places on the relationship. Many of today’s Boomer mothers were once the daughters in research like this, navigating the same tug-of-war with their own mothers. They haven't forgotten that. They're trying to discern how to manage things well with their own daughters, but sometimes it still comes off poorly.

Sources indicate that that is the boundary conversation in a nutshell. A daughter may be focused on protecting her time, energy, and independence. Her mother is at a stage of life when she is intensely focused on family ties. She's laser-focused on keeping the relationship close, but maybe doesn't have the skills to make it happen, just the desire for it to be so. Both daughter and mother are responding to real needs. They just aren’t the same needs.

And nowhere does that mismatch become more visible than during the holidays, when traditions, expectations, and family identities are on full display.

Sources indicate that as a family communication researcher, I’ve spent more than a decade studying the invisible work of daughtering: the task, emotional, cognitive, and identity labor adult daughters do to keep families connected. Lately, I’ve become especially interested in what happens when daughters begin to renegotiate that work.

In a recent development, boundary conflict isn’t really about what a daughter is willing to do or a wall she's putting in place with her mother. The tension is about what these boundaries end up meaning to everyone else. A daughter's work (or lack thereof) ripples to every corner of the family. When she decides to prioritize some needs more than others and set down some of the unnecessary labor she's been doing, expect the family to shift, either seismically or gently, but it will change nonetheless. But you should know, daughter, you have every right not to abandon yourself and your needs. Set the boundary, but don't be shocked when others dislike it or feel hurt. Wait it out with empathy and gentle understanding. A latest paradigm is on the horizon.

Sources indicate that centorrino, M., & Ferrigno, C. (2026). Memetic narratives of generational conflict: The “boomers vs. millennials” frame on Instagram. Journalism and Media, 7(3), 187. https://www.mdpi.com/2673-5172/7/3/187.

It has been revealed that birditt, K. S., Hartnett, C. S., Fingerman, K. L., Zarit, S., & Antonucci, T. C. (2015). Extending the intergenerational stake hypothesis: Evidence of an intraindividual stake and implications for well-being. Journal of Marriage and Family, 77(4), 877–888. https://doi.org/10.1111/jomf.12203.

Sources indicate that fingerman, K. L. (1996). Sources of tension in the aging mother and adult daughter relationship. Psychology and Aging, 11(4), 591–606. https://doi.org/10.1037/0882-7974.11.4.591.

6 to 8 Cups of Tea Daily May Reduce Heart Disease Risk by 11%

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (628 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People who regularly drink tea may have an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease, which includes conditions such as stroke, heart disease, and peripheral artery disease.
  • It has been revealed that both black tea and green tea may offer heart health benefits.
  • The lowest overall vascular risk was seen among tea drinkers who were also physically active and didn’t smoke.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People who regularly drink tea may have an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease, which includes conditions such as stroke, heart disease, and peripheral artery disease. This is according to a study published on October 21 in the Journal of Internal Medicine.

It has been revealed that both black tea and green tea may offer heart health benefits. However, the study demonstrates an association rather than proving that drinking tea prevents cardiovascular disease.

The lowest overall vascular risk was seen among tea drinkers who were also physically active and didn’t smoke.

The study followed 485,934 people ages 30–79 from the China Kadoorie Biobank for an average of 9 years.

According to recent reports, the researchers found that regular tea drinkers had an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease compared with those who did not regularly drink tea. They also observed a 37% lower risk of ischemic stroke and a 17% lower risk of heart attack.

There was no clear link for hemorrhagic stroke or pulmonary heart disease.

Recent findings suggest that among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk was seen in those consuming approximately 6–8 cups per day. However, the findings do not establish this as a recommended daily intake.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist with Manhattan Cardiology in NYC who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that it is vital to remember this is observational data.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining the effects of drinking black and green tea on lipids and blood pressure showed only modest, non-significant benefits.

The study also had limitations, including self-reported tea consumption and the possibility that other dietary and lifestyle factors influenced the results.

“Overall, tea seems to, maybe, have some cardiovascular benefits without a significant risk, so I favor tea consumption,” he said.

Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished who was not involved in the research, emphasized that the findings do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship between drinking tea and a lower risk of vascular disease.

“Tea can be a helpful addition to a heart-healthy lifestyle, but it is not a substitute for addressing individual cardiovascular risk factors,” she noted.

The researchers also found that drinking “burning hot” tea increased the risk of vascular disease by 16%, consistent with previous research raising concerns about the consumption of very hot beverages.

“I recommend enjoying your tea’s potential benefits by letting it cool to a comfortable sipping temperature before you drink it,” said Routhenstein.

The study examined black, green, Oolong, and other tea types.

Industry observers note that the researchers found that black tea highlighted a more consistent association with a lower risk of vascular disease, which is contrary to some earlier research. However, they noted that these results don’t establish black tea as superior to green tea, and they don’t mean you should switch tea types.

“Both black and green tea are great choices for your heart health, and neither is definitively better than the other,” said Routhenstein.

“I recommend choosing whichever you enjoy and consuming it consistently, ideally without much added sugar,” Routhenstein noted.

Blumfield also noted that adding sugar or non-sugar sweeteners may change the potential health effects of drinking tea, so the findings should not automatically be extended to sweetened tea beverages.

Some older research suggests there may be additional health benefits to drinking both black and green tea. These benefits may include:.

Routhenstein said that tea may also support focus and alertness, improve hydration status, and potentially play a role in metabolic health.

“Enjoying tea can be a simple way to incorporate beneficial plant compounds into your day,” she added.

While drinking tea has been considered a health-promoting habit since ancient times, more research is needed to confirm its various health benefits.

China’s electric airliner era starts with a 19-seat plane and 400 km of range

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong.
  • The CE-25A had already completed 19 autonomous test flights with nobody on board since February 2, and China’s aviation regulator is now reviewing it for a type certificate.
  • According to recent reports, the CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong. Two pilots and a flight test engineer were aboard the roughly 10-tonne demonstrator, and COMAC claims every system worked normally.

It wasn’t the plane’s first flight. The CE-25A had already completed 19 autonomous test flights with nobody on board since February 2, and China’s aviation regulator is now reviewing it for a type certificate.

According to recent reports, the CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers. COMAC lists a 300 km/h cruise speed and a 400 km (250-mile) range.

The CAAC accepting COMAC’s type certificate application starts the airworthiness review. It doesn’t mean paying passengers are close, and COMAC hasn’t given a date for commercial service.

The program has been quiet for a long time. COMAC showed a CE-25A model at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai in November 2023, with a placard listing 400 to 500 km of range and a 400 km/h top cruise speed. The full-size aircraft, registered B-0EFH, only became public when photos leaked on Chinese social media on October 28.

The obvious battery candidate is CATL. In July 2023, COMAC, CATL, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University formed a joint venture with CNY 600 million in registered capital to develop electric aircraft, as we reported when CATL launched its aviation unit.

CATL had just unveiled its “condensed” battery at the time, claiming up to 500 Wh/kg at the cell level, and said it was testing the cells to aviation standards. Neither company has confirmed what’s inside the CE-25A, though.

~500 Wh/kg has long been seen as the target for battery energy density to enable electric flight on a commercial scale.

COMAC isn’t alone in flying a large electric demonstrator. In August, Heart Aerospace flew its X1 in Plattsburgh, New York, for 27 minutes. It’s a 25,000-lb aircraft with a 106-foot wingspan, which Heart calls the largest battery-electric aircraft ever flown.

Eviation flew its 9-passenger Alice back in September 2022, then laid off most of its staff in early 2025.

Industry observers note that heart is the closest Western comparison. It dropped its 19-seat ES-19 for the 30-seat ES-30 back in 2022, and the ES-30 now relies on reserve turbogenerators to stretch its range, with BAE Systems working on the battery. Heart is targeting 2031 for service and claims “more than 40%” lower operating costs.

In a recent development, for years, the go-to excuse in the West for doing nothing about emissions was China. Why should we bother, the argument went, if China won’t? Now China is pulling ahead, and it’s doing it by cutting its dependence on fossil fuels.

Look at trucking. Electric trucks hit 50.3% of China’s heavy truck sales in September, and they’re already eating into the country’s diesel demand. In the US, electric models were about 0.3% of heavy-truck sales last year, according to the ICCT.

A great step in the right direction, probably needs a doubling in range but at current rates of progress that will only be five years away.

It has been revealed that now it’s planes, starting where batteries make sense today: short regional routes. The CE-25A’s 400 km shrinks once you keep the reserves regulators require, and a Beechcraft 1900 turboprop in the same class covers well over 1,000 km. So it’s not replacing turboprops anytime soon. But that’s how trucking started too. Short-haul first, then long-haul tractors once the batteries caught up.

And this couldn’t happen fast enough. We’re in the middle of a diesel and jet fuel crisis. Jet fuel averaged $3.50 a gallon in early August, up 63% from a year earlier, according to Heart Aerospace. Every truck and plane China moves to batteries is one less exposed to that.

Industry observers note that china also has the batteries to pull it off, with CATL in the joint venture. Meanwhile, Heart has pushed to 2031 and added a fuel-burning backup, and Eviation is a cautionary tale.

The Best Men's Boots, Tested by Style Editors

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I DIDN’T START out as a “boot guy.” I always thought they were clunky, poorly stitched and didn’t provide enough insole support like my favorite Nike Air Force 1s.
  • Since then, the Men’s Health style team and I have tested well over 50 pairs across every silhouette imaginable: cowboy boots, hiking boots, waterproof commuters, dressier Chelsea styles, heritage work boots—the whole lineup.
  • According to recent reports, the iconic Blundstone #585 still reigns supreme for its comfort, durability, and style.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I DIDN’T START out as a “boot guy.” I always thought they were clunky, poorly stitched and didn’t provide enough insole support like my favorite Nike Air Force 1s. But 15 years ago, I bought my first pair of Timberland 6-Inch Premium Boots because a brutal winter hit the East Coast, and slipping around in sneakers wasn’t going to cut it. I needed something that could survive the rain, snow, and slush. It didn’t take long to realize that once fall hits, having a solid pair (or two) in rotation is a non-negotiable. That first leather lace-up carried me through snowball fights and more than a few questionable bar floors—and it sold me on what a good boot can do.

Since then, the Men’s Health style team and I have tested well over 50 pairs across every silhouette imaginable: cowboy boots, hiking boots, waterproof commuters, dressier Chelsea styles, heritage work boots—the whole lineup. I’ve worn them on shoots, to weddings, on rainy office days, and on long travel runs, and I can confirm: not every boot is bulky. The right pair can feel as clean and sleek as your favorite sneakers. So if you’re looking for something versatile enough to move from the office to the bar or carry you from one event to the next, we’ve got you covered. Our picks deliver comfort, durability, and style, whether you need a tough trail option, something practical for wet commutes, or a sleek pair for a night out.

According to recent reports, the iconic Blundstone #585 still reigns supreme for its comfort, durability, and style. Part Chelsea boot, part work boot, its leather feels soft with a pre-distressed texture, while inside is cushy and snug from the moment you put it on. We didn’t feel any tightness or have to wait a couple of wears for it to mold to our feet. Our editor Tim Kohut wears it at his standing desk for seven hours straight, and his feet never give in or develop blisters. He even took it on a weekend hike and felt comfortable the whole way, hills, dips, and all. The pull tabs also make it easy to slide your foot in and out.

Industry observers note that I’ve worn warmer boots in my testing, but they were much bulkier. This pair has a lighter, slimmer build, yet works for general fall and winter gear. The boot’s leather upper dries in minutes, whether I get caught in light showers or trudge through three inches of snow. Yes, the material can scuff if you’re not careful, but a quick wipe with a damp cloth brings it right back. After months of near-daily wear, the elastic panels haven’t stretched out, the sole hasn’t flattened, and the leather has developed a natural patina versus looking beat up. Underfoot, the synthetic polyurethane midsole feels like a thick layer of cushioning, softening every step, especially on Newly introduced York’s uneven sidewalks.

In the toe area, my feet have wiggle room instead of feeling cramped. Whether for style or performance, this boot works in a variety of settings. I’ve worn mine with a sweater and dark denim for dinner as well as chinos for the office, and it pairs seamlessly with any casual staples like a flannel overshirt, tee, and jeans under a fall jacket. The price tag may give you pause, but most boots that I’ve spent over $100 on are worth it. You don’t have to baby this one. It looks good as new after being worn everywhere, so it’s a reliable option for work, travel, and trail.

Read More: Blundstone 585 Chelsea Boot Review.

Industry observers note that when our senior fitness and commerce editor Brett Williams slipped into the Beckett Simonon Bolton Chelsea, he immediately called out how sharp it looked. This Chelsea boot—a style originating in 19th-century Britain as a close-fitting riding boot with elastic side panels—elevates whatever you’re wearing. The super premium, full-grain calfskin leather has a natural sheen and structure, and the almond-shaped toe box gives it a sleek profile that reads dressy. Inside, the Vachetta leather lining helped keep his foot cool and surprisingly comfortable after hours at his standing desk.

Brett wore it with suits, dress pants, and black denim on shoot days, and it held up across the board. And yes, Chelseas aren’t strictly “formal only” anymore, but the Bolton proves that a dress-leaning Chelsea can still be incredibly versatile. The stitched construction makes it lighter and more flexible than the typical Goodyear-welted options. It’s easily one of the best leather Chelsea boots on the market because it nails every detail: premium calfskin, a breathable lining, a sleek silhouette, and real comfort. Plenty of Chelseas look the part but feel clunky or overly stiff, so the $279 is justifiable.

Read More: Best Chelsea Boots for Men.

Sources indicate that our grooming editor, Sean Zucker, took the Amberjack Chukka for a proper test run, and he came back raving about how wildly comfortable it felt from the jump. The full-grain leather upper and sheepskin lining give it a polished look, but the real magic is underfoot: the heat-activated insole that molds to your feet after a few wears. Plus, the lightweight outsole feels closer to a cushy sneaker than a traditional boot.

Industry observers note that sean wore it on rainy commutes, into the office, and around the city on weekend errands. He didn’t have any sore arches or slips on wet sidewalks. The leather ages nicely over time, and the overall vibe lands squarely in that “smart casual” sweet spot. It works with chinos and slim trousers, and can stretch to dark denim, but it’s not meant to stand in for a dress boot.

If you’ve dismissed cowboy boots as too costumey, Tecovas offers a sleek option that balances rugged style and pairs with a bunch of casual and dressy fits. The round-toe design features a tough, beautiful cowhide leather that wears well whether you’re dressing up or down. The cowhide leather gives the Cartwright a durable feel, while its classic round toe and signature stitching keep the design recognizable.

In a recent development, surprisingly, I didn’t have to break this boot in. From the first wear, it felt comfortable without any pinching or stiffness. To coincide with the theme, I wore it to Beyoncé’s Cowboy Carter concert in Upcoming Jersey, and I stood the entire three hours. During the first half of the show, it started lightly raining, but the leather dried in seconds. While it’s not as grippy on slippery surfaces as the Merrell and Timberland boots, it’s stable enough for most city sidewalks. Our editors found it to be suitable for the office, the bar, or even a wedding. It’s one of those boots that you can wear year-round. Tecovas offers a few different colors, but we’re especially into the hazelnut, which looks great with dark jeans or dressier pants.

What really makes this Tecovas pair stand out is how approachable it feels, especially if you’ve never owned a cowboy boot before. The 12-inch shaft—the part of the boot that rises from your ankle to your lower calf—isn’t overly tall or stiff, so it slips easily under straight or relaxed-fit jeans. Also, the 1½-inch heel is low and manageable, so you get a classic cowboy shape without feeling like you’re walking on a block. Fit-wise, it runs true to size and feels secure without squeezing the instep, which is often the biggest concern with Western-style boots. If you want the look without committing to something flashy or trend-driven, this is a smart, low-risk entry point that still feels elevated.

Timberland’s classic work boot has outlasted trendy styles for decades because it’s durable, has a timeless design, and goes with everything. Aptly named the “Butters”, it’s one of the most recognizable boots because of its signature cut and proportions: the high top, thick lug sole, and warm wheat-colored nubuck leather. It’s become a staple across music, streetwear and sports culture. I’ve had it in rotation since I was a teen and still weave it into my casual fits to this day. Yes, it takes one to three wears to break in, but after that you get a snug, customized fit that you can fine-tune with the laces.

The Timberland boot’s cultural relevance hasn’t slowed down, either. A lot of fashion gents like Timothée Chalamet have been spotted wearing Timberland off-duty and even at red carpet events. It also taps into today’s men’s trends, especially the ongoing ’90s-Y2K revival, where baggier denim, boxy jackets, and easy, layered knits are back in rotation.

Sources indicate that this boot has full-grain and nubuck leather uppers that can handle scuffs and are fully waterproof, so rain and slush never ruin the look. It's sturdier and heavier than most fashion boots, because it was originally built for work, but it doesn't feel like you’re lugging around bricks all day. The bulk is part of the style, and why it pairs so well with relaxed denim, cargos, and winter fits. Whether I’m walking on wet sidewalks or cobblestone, the lug sole feels stable underfoot.

Recent findings suggest that if we’re judging purely on trail performance, the Merrell Thermo Chill 2 is the best pick for hiking. The mid-height design gives your ankles the extra support they need on uneven terrain, so you’re not wobbling around. Most hiking boot outsoles rely on standard rubber compounds that work well, but they usually sacrifice grip for durability or flexibility. With 200g insulation, this style makes for a perfect winter boot.

It’s fully waterproof, so puddles, rain, or soggy grass aren’t going to slow you down. The main draw here is the exclusive footbed, which molds to your foot, over time, giving each step a cushioned, natural feel. Brower wore this boot on a weekend camping trip, splashing through soggy trails and wet grass, and by the end of it, his feet were dry and comfortable. The mesh on the tongue keeps things breathable, too, so when the sun comes out, your feet don’t feel like they’re baking. While it’s not as sleek as the Danner boot, it’s still a solid-looking boot that you can wear off the trail.

According to recent reports, most rugged boots are kind of ugly, but Danner delivers a trail-ready option that actually looks sharp. The rich tan color paired with red laces gives it a bold yet unique look for the trail. Outside of hikes, our Tech and Gear editor Ryan Brower likes to style it with a flannel shirt and jeans. He’s been wearing it consistently over the last couple fall seasons. It’s not the warmest option in freezing 30-degree temps, so it might be wise to wear with thicker socks. It’s made with full-grain leather uppers, which age beautifully and bead off rain. Plus, the waterproof liners keep water from getting inside.

Full-grain leather is also tougher and more durable than corrected grain or split leather (found in cheaper boots) that have been sanded or split down, losing their outer layers. The break-in period takes a little patience, but after a few wears, this boot feels comfortable and natural. The Vibram outsole grips especially well on uneven terrain, whether you’re climbing trails in the Oregon mountains or navigating slick city streets in Newly introduced York. Between the outsole and insole, there’s a fiberglass shank—a thin, supportive layer that reinforces the midfoot. It helps keep your feet stable, prevents the boot from twisting, and reduces fatigue on long walks.

Industry observers note that red Wing has been crafting durable, American-made workwear for more than a century, supplying tradesmen, factory workers and miners with boots built to last. The Classic Moc Boot continues that tradition with a roomy moc toe, weatherproof leather construction, and a comfortable wedge sole that makes long hours on your feet far more manageable. (A moc toe is a stitched toe design where the seam wraps around the front of the boot, giving extra room and durability.).

Industry observers note that men’s Health designer Jason Speakman broke it in on a hike in upstate Newly introduced York. Since the leather is a bit hefty, it did take some getting used to. But after about two or three wears, he said it didn’t feel as cramped as other moc toe boots he's tested. There was no strain on his feet after going from rocks to packed trails, and they stayed comfortable even on uneven terrain. Aesthetically, it has the rugged, All-American vibe that works on a job site, weekend trail, or just rolling up to the beer hall in jeans. The full-grain oiled leather is super premium, so this option will last years and develop a cool, worn-in patina.

In a recent development, after doing some work in the yard for hours on end, Speakman found the EVA midsole—which is a foam material that’s both lightweight and strong—makes this boot the most comfortable option for raking leaves and pushing a lawnmower. It also handles hard surfaces like concrete or brick, keeping your feet cushioned and protected from constant pounding.

It has been revealed that if you’re looking for a hiking boot that won’t make your wallet flinch but still performs like something far more expensive, the Nortiv8’s offering is an easy win. On the trail it proved, while affordable, that it’s not cheaply made. Right out of the box, the waterproof synthetic leather and textile upper felt surprisingly substantial—not floppy or flimsy like some lower-cost boots. The material stood up to brush and rocks on a muddy forest loop, and after hours of hauling gear and setting up camp in wet grass, it still looked crisp with no signs of fraying.

The waterproof membrane lived up to its promise during shallow creek crossings and soggy morning hikes; my socks stayed dry every time, even when water pooled around my feet. Underfoot, the rubber lug outsole delivered dependable traction. I tested it while fishing and the grip felt stable and sturdy. The midsole’s cushioned EVA foam struck a nice balance too: supportive on long miles but soft enough that my feet didn’t feel trashed by day’s end. It’s not an ultralight trail runner, but for hiking, camping, fishing, and general outdoor wear, the way these materials work together is impressive for the price.

It has been revealed that not many boots can pull off a tailored suit, but Frye’s luxe ankle style is the rare exception. I’ve been wearing mine for the past couple months, and it instantly makes any semi-formal fit feel sharper. The design is simple but polished with a premium leather upper and is stitched around the edge for extra durability. I wore it in light rain and the material dried in seconds. I also found the inner-side zipper makes life so much easier when I’m slipping it on and off after a long day. It was refreshing that it didn’t require an annoying break-in period. When I first tried it on, I realized I had wiggle room in the toe area right away.

After five wears, the leather starts to crease naturally, but that adds personality to the boot without it looking worn. I’ve tested it on city streets and light rain, and the grip is solid enough to feel confident walking anywhere without slipping or scuffing the leather. The ankle height is flattering, the shape is not heavy-looking, and the richness of the leather colors pairs with different outfits. You can rock jeans and a sweater for a casual lunch, or dress it up with slacks and a blazer.

Sure, this boot isn’t cheap, but the quality, durability, and timeless design make it worth the investment. You’re paying for a boot that will remain in good condition for years, look better as it ages, and feel comfortable from day one.

It has been revealed that leather is a reliable choice for everyday boots because it can be durable and develop character with wear. Full-grain and nubuck each have their own look and feel, but neither guarantees waterproof protection on its own. If you’re regularly walking through rain or slush, look for a waterproof membrane or specifically waterproof construction.

It has been revealed that EVA foam midsoles are lightweight and cushioned, perfect for long days on your feet. Some boots use polyurethane midsoles, which are a bit heavier but offer more durability and stability, especially if you’re on rugged terrain.

Your traction and durability depend on this part. Vibram outsoles are often considered the gold standard for their grip and long-lasting wear. Rubber outsoles are common on everyday and outdoor boots because they can provide traction and abrasion resistance. Grip varies by rubber compound and tread pattern, so look for an outsole designed for the surfaces and conditions you’ll encounter.

Goodyear-welted boots can be a good investment because their construction often allows the outsole to be replaced when it wears down. The welt can also help limit water intrusion, although the construction alone doesn’t make a boot waterproof.

Our fashion team, led by longtime boots enthusiast and Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, found the most comfortable and durable options out there. We put more than 50 pairs of boots through the wringer, wearing them across cobblestone Upcoming York streets, rainy city commutes, long-distance hikes, and casual weekends around town. In each test, we looked closely at grip, how the soles handled slick surfaces, insulation to keep feet warm in cold weather, and waterproofing to make sure soggy socks weren’t part of the deal. We also rewarded boots that could pull double duty: looking sharp with dress pants or a suit while still holding up for more rugged, off-duty wear.

#29695. Latest Update: Driving the Scion Kei Truck: Fun, But Not a Real Solution for Most Americans

Latest Update: Driving the Scion Kei Truck: Fun, But Not a Real Solution for Most Americans

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (964 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that what started as a government-subsidized program to provide cheap, industrious transportation for a Japanese economy that had been ravaged by World War II has become a genuine American fixation.
  • As with all vehicles not originally built to U.S.
  • Officially known as the Scion by Toyota Kei-01, the rebadged Daihatsu Hijet is powered by a 660-cc three-cylinder gasoline engine making around 53 hp, which is fed through a continuously variable automatic transmission.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that what started as a government-subsidized program to provide cheap, industrious transportation for a Japanese economy that had been ravaged by World War II has become a genuine American fixation. In mountainous resort towns in Colorado, Faulkner farmland in the Delta, and Northeast metropolises, the pint-size Kei truck has become a popular target for importers bringing examples from Japan. Now Toyota is set to dump fuel on that fire, as a brand-new kei truck from the resurrected Scion brand will be offered in the U.S. market in 2027.

As with all vehicles not originally built to U.S. standards, federal Department of Transportation rules have limited American kei enthusiasts to importing 25-year-old examples of the miniature trucks. To be frank, most of these tired examples drive as one would expect of a work truck with a quarter century under its belt. Toyota’s incoming example is the exact opposite, as I got the chance to find out during a half-dozen laps of a half-mile cone course at Eagles Canyon Raceway outside Dallas.

Officially known as the Scion by Toyota Kei-01, the rebadged Daihatsu Hijet is powered by a 660-cc three-cylinder gasoline engine making around 53 hp, which is fed through a continuously variable automatic transmission. The Kei-01 is limited to 25 mph, far short of the 70 mph or so a Japanese-market Hijet can accomplish. That threshold was deliberately chosen to comply with federal safety requirements for low-speed vehicles, which mandate that the vehicle go faster than 20 mph but not faster than 25.

According to recent reports, yet that modest limit didn’t mean acceleration was lacking. When I moved the hilariously toylike shifter into drive and matted the gas, the Kei-01 jumped off the line like a puppy smelling sausages, growling and uncoordinated. The lack of gear ratios kept the tiny engine at high rpm, although the missing tach meant I couldn’t verify how fast it was spinning. Regardless, maximum speed was easily reached, according to the speedometer displaying kilometers per hour.

Industry observers note that the ergonomics of a kei truck meant I sat on top of the front wheels and had the Toyota-badged steering wheel tilted into my lap. Also, this being a product designed for the Japanese market, the steering wheel was positioned on the right; Toyota has no prepares to reverse the layout for us. With 14-inch wheels and what are barely soccer-ball-diameter tires, the Kei-01 was agile to a fault; I suspect you could pretty much turn it inside a single Costco parking space. Directional changes happened rapidly, although the steering is high geared, and even slow-speed maneuvers elicited a special charm. That mentioned, I wouldn’t want to haul it around a tight corner at any rate of speed. And the ride quality could be described generously as rudimentary. I bounced up and down in my adjustable seat over Toyota’s provided gravel course, the interior loudly rattling the whole time. However, as a dedicated work truck, this was hardly disqualifying.

Recent findings suggest that A button in the center console promised locking four-wheel-drive, though I didn’t get to use it. Slowing the Kei-01, with its curb weight of just over 2000 pounds, was as easy as letting off the accelerator. But front disc and rear drum brakes seemed powerful enough. Considering the modest limiter, you could just yank the analog, wire-operated parking brake.

Toyota hasn’t skimped on features. A central touchscreen tucked into the dashboard will supposedly have Apple CarPlay functionality when the Kei-01 arrives in the U.S. next year. Push-button start and slider-style climate controls will also be fitted as standard. For those who have bemoaned the rise of haptic-touch features, the Kei-01 will be the freshest breath of interior design air you’ve had in some time. Icons on the Kei-01’s dashboard even promised ADAS features like lane-departure control and collision warnings. Some of the touch surfaces were hard, and the doors felt featherlight, but who really cares?

Recent findings suggest that the Kei-01’s payload capacity, scaled to its diminutive dimensions, is just 600 pounds. But the three sides of the load bed can be folded down separately, boosting utility, meaning that trips to Home Depot are more likely to be limited by speed than cargo weight. A storage deck behind the seats is well suited for backpacks and toolboxes, and there are flat storage spaces on the dashboard and built into the roofline.

Before you check your credit score, there is a brutal catch to the possibility of buying the Kei-01. Toyota has stated it won’t sell the vehicle to individuals initially, with access limited to fleet operators.

Industry observers note that the plan is to target luxury resorts, university administrations, and other institutions with the need for such compact utility. This makes sense given both the likely lack of profit in individual trucks and the logic of putting the trucks into the hands of what are likely to be safe, responsible customers with their own private road networks. Toyota hasn’t revealed pricing yet, but the Kei-01 will almost certainly carry a sizable upcharge over the equivalent Hijet, which costs about $9000 in Japan, with U.S. versions being built in Indiana.

The brutal truth is that a maximum speed of 25 mph means the Scion Kei-01 simply isn’t suited to road use in much of the U.S. Even in the center of cities like Latest York, where speed limits are largely set at that number, traffic normally flows considerably faster when free to do so. The prospect of trying to drive a Kei-01 on a faster-flowing highway surrounded by inattentive traffic is slightly terrifying. Toyota’s decision to keep the bulk of Kei-01s away from public roads is prudent, if a little disappointing. I’ve never had more fun going 25 mph.

High altitude, bitter cold, zero drivers: autonomous trucks take on Tibetan mine

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.

Recent findings suggest that chinese equipment brand SANY has deployed fully 60 of its 70-tonne (~80 ton) payload-rated SKT105ED battery electric haul trucks at the Zhibula Copper Mine in Tibet. Operated by Zijin Minig and Tibet Julong Copper, the mine functions at a dizzying 17,700 foot elevation in a region of the Gangdese Mountains known as the Kailas Range, and the conditions there would challenge the health and safety of even the toughest and fittest operators.

“High-altitude illness becomes increasingly relevant above 2,500 meters,” explains Eacon, in one section of a published paper. “Research involving workers in Andes mines operating between 3,800 and 4,500 meters found that 73% of workers assessed experienced periods of nocturnal oxygen saturation below 85% during their high-altitude shifts, indicating moderate-to-severe hypoxemia.”.

That’s bad news for Zijin’s workers – but the good news here, of course, is that the manufacturer won’t be needing many heavy haul drivers going forward.

SANY has been working with Perth, Australia-based Eacon Mining Technology to develop an autonomous haulage solution that uses a full suite of both in-vehicle and ground-based sensors, adaptive vehicle controls, and machine learning that can handle the significant bad trucks even here in the Kailas range.

“Autonomous haulage offers one way to address this challenge,” continues the Econ report. “Rather than requiring a driver for each truck, autonomous systems allow fleets to be managed through centralized supervision, with personnel overseeing operations and intervening when required. This reduces the need for people to spend entire shifts operating equipment at elevation, while changing how workforce resources are allocated across the mine … depending on the system configuration, some operations can manage autonomous fleets from remote Integrated Operations Centers located away from the mine site, (allowing) personnel to supervise haulage activities from lower-altitude locations, further reducing the need for workers to remain in extreme-altitude environments.”.

The working partnership between the two companies combines SANY’s battery-powered truck platform with Eacon’s full technology stack to create dependable, driverless haul trucks with logic and behaviors that are ideally suited to China’s open-pit mining environments.

Eacon technology is currently operating more than 3,100 autonomous trucks cross more than 40 large-scale mines, including Zijin Mining’s Zijinshan Gold-Copper Mine and at the Norton Gold Fields project in Australia.

Industry observers note that while specifications for this specific deployment weren’t disclosed, the SANY SKT105E trucks (the “D” is, presumably, the wide-body variant) the company has deployed elsewhere are powered by a dual-motor electric drivetrain, pairing two permanent-magnet synchronous motors with a dual three-speed automated manual transmission. The system delivers 570 kW (~765 hp) of continuous power and up to 820 kW (~1,100 hp) at peak output, with each motor producing some 2,430 Nm (~18,00 lb-ft) of peak torque.

Those motors get their electrons from an absolute whopper of a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack in capacities ranging from 423 to 642 kWh, depending on configuration. The big trucks also offer regenerative braking to recover energy on downhill runs, while their fast-charging system can reportedly charge the battery from 20% to 90% in under an hour.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it seems straight out of a Disney movie—wild animals from two different species becoming inseparable friends.
  • Last spring, the wildlife center received two likely orphaned turkey poults (young turkeys).
  • “Since we never raise baby animals alone, we had to find a companion for the remaining poult,” the wildlife center wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it seems straight out of a Disney movie—wild animals from two different species becoming inseparable friends. And yet that’s what happened at the Raven Ridge Wildlife Center in southeastern Pennsylvania, between a turkey and a mourning dove.

Last spring, the wildlife center received two likely orphaned turkey poults (young turkeys). To calm them down, the team put them with a feather-duster as a stand-in mother turkey. Because turkey poults are easily stressed, they are difficult to rehabilitate, according to a Facebook post by the wildlife center. In fact, one of them didn’t make it.

“Since we never raise baby animals alone, we had to find a companion for the remaining poult,” the wildlife center wrote. “We paired it with a baby mourning dove of similar size, hoping they would comfort each other while eating and exploring as they are both ground eaters.”.

The pairing turned out to be a raging success. They formed an inseparable bond that Raven Ridge Wildlife Center had never seen before. Months later, the team gave the dove a soft release, meaning the bird could leave whenever it wanted. But he clearly had no intention of leaving his friend. The dove continued returning to the turkey’s cage, and the two would sit near each other on either side of the separation.

According to recent reports, “After a few days, we put the dove back in with the turkey, and it was clear they were happiest together,” the wildlife center explained. But “we knew keeping them caged for the rest of their lives, or keeping them just because they were cute, was neither an option nor fair to these wild animals.”.

In a recent development, as such, the team contacted a large sanctuary in Pennsylvania to request a joint release. This way, the duo could choose whether to stick together or follow their own paths. After their soft release, the dove flew into the trees and the turkey started foraging, free to stick together or join other members of their species.

“We don’t know if they’ll stay together, but our team made sure they had a safe place until they were ready to be on their own,” the wildlife center concluded.
